newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NRG, CMS seen as Loy Yang A buyer.
newsitem.headline: NRG, CMS seen as Loy Yang A buyer.

text.p: A consortium led by U.S. utilities NRG Energy Inc and CMS Energy Corp are believed to have won the bidding for Australia's state-owned Loy Yang A power station, sources close to the bidding said on Monday.
The winning bid would be announced on Tuesday by the Victoria state government, they said.

The 2,000 megawatt coal-fired station and an associated coal mine are expected to fetch around A$4.5 billion in what would be the nation's single biggest privatisation. The NRG-CMS consortium also includes Australian investment bank Macquarie Bank via the vehicle Horizon Energy Investments.
The NRG-CMS-Macquarie consortium was competing against two consortia led by the American Electric Power Co Inc (AEP) and by another U.S. utility, AES Corp (AES).
The AEP consortium includes China Light and Power Co Ltd, a source told Reuters.
"At this stage, there's no formal notification from the state," said David Scaysbrook, managing director of NRG's Australian subsidiary, NRG Australia Ltd.
"We are waiting with nervous anticipation and we hope to have something, some notification, tomorrow or the next day."
Sources close to the bidding said the NRG-CMS-Macquarie consortium would be announced as winning bidder on Tuesday.
A spokesman for the state government declined to comment.
The Victoria government has so far sold over A$13 billion worth of electricity assets in an effort to retire debt and to create a competitive power industry.
The sale of Loy Yang A, the biggest and most modern of Victoria's electricity assets to go on the block so far, was initially expected to be sold for about A$5 billion.
But recent rises in long-term interest rates as well as aggressive competition from state-owned power generators in New South Wales state have pared this back to around A$4.5 billion.

If Loy Yang A does succeed in fetching over A$5 billion, the sale would then rank above the national government's sale of its half stake in the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) last year as the nation's biggest single privatisation.
The CBA sale fetched about A$5 billion.
Victoria's electricity assets have attracted premium prices due to the state's efficient brown coal resources and as a way into Australia's emerging national market for electricity.
The Victoria and New South Wales electricity markets formally merge late this month, when electricity will be freely traded across state borders.
But New South Wales generators, all state owned, have already begun undercutting lower-cost competitors in Victoria, said industry analyst Harry Perry of NUS International.
"The feeling is that the New South Wales generators are pushing the price lower than it ought to be," Perry said.
